scenes.title: Introduction to Apache Kafka
scenes.subtitle: The distributed event streaming platform
scenes.narration: Apache Kafka is a distributed, fault-tolerant platform for publishing, storing, and processing streams of events at massive scale.

scenes.title: What Kafka Provides
scenes.narration: At its heart Kafka is a durable, append-only commit log that stores every event on disk. It offers publish and subscribe messaging so producers and consumers stay decoupled. It scales horizontally by spreading data across many brokers. And unlike a plain queue, Kafka retains history so consumers can replay past events at any time.

scenes.title: The Kafka Data Flow
scenes.narration: A producer sends events to Kafka without knowing who will read them. Brokers store those events durably inside topics. Consumers subscribe and read events at their own pace, and each consumer tracks its position with an offset. This decoupling lets many independent applications share the same stream.

scenes.title: Publishing a Message
scenes.code:
# Start a console producer and send events
kafka-console-producer.sh \
  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \
  --topic orders

# Type a message and press Enter
> {"order_id": 101, "amount": 29.99}
scenes.narration: You can interact with Kafka directly from the command line. Here the console producer connects to a broker on port 9092 and targets the orders topic. Each line you type is published as a separate event. This same pattern underlies production client libraries in Java, Python, and other languages.

scenes.title: Kafka vs a Database
scenes.narration: A database stores the current state of things and lets you query it on demand, updating records in place. Kafka instead stores the ongoing stream of changes as immutable events and pushes them forward to interested consumers. Together they complement each other, with Kafka often feeding databases and other systems.

scenes.text: Kafka became the backbone of modern data platforms because it decouples systems, scales horizontally, and lets teams build on a shared, replayable stream of events.
